1. Delay condoned.
2. The respondent no.1/ Kuljinder Singh, although served
with the notice issued by this Court yet has chosen not to
remain present before this Court either in person or through
an advocate and oppose this petition.
3. Leave granted.
4. These appeals arise from the order passed by the High
Court  of  Punjab  &  Haryana  dated  15.02.2025  in  CRM-M-
27027/2016  by  which  the  application  preferred  by  the
respondent no.1/accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh seeking quashing
of the proceedings arising from complaint no.9117/2014 for
the offence punishable under Section 138 of the Negotiable
Instruments Act (for short, ‘the NI Act’) which came to be
quashed.
5. The appellant before us is the original complainant. He
lodged  a  private  complaint  in  the  Court  of  the  Chief
1

--- Page 48 ---
Metropolitan  Magistrate,  Chandigarh,  for  the  offence
punishable under Section 138 of the NI Act which came to be
registered  as  complaint  case  no.9117/2014.  In  the  said
complaint, the respondent no.1 before us is arrayed as
accused no.2. The accused no.1 is the private limited company
of which the respondent no.1/accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh is
one of the Directors along with the respondent no.2/accused
no.3/Yadvinder  Singh  and  the  respondent  no.3/accused
no.4/Ajit Singh (deceased). According to the complaint, the
accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh is the signatory to the cheque
in question, whereas, the accused nos.3&4 had also played key
role in the subject transaction, respectively. The complaint
reads thus:-
“1. That the complainant is a Pvt. Ltd. Company duly
incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, having its
registered office at the address aforesaid i.e. Mr.
Sanjay Jain, Director of the complainant company, vide
Resolution of Board of Directors of complainant company
dated 30.05.2014, is duly authorized to file and sign the
present complaint, pleadings, vakalatnamas, applications,
etc., engage lawyers, etc. and to do all such acts
necessary  for  the  proper  conduct  of  the  present
complaint.
2. That the accused No.1 is a Pvt. Ltd. company having
its registered office at Opposite Indus Tower, IIIrd
Floor, DLF IT Park, Chandigarh-160001. The accused Nos.2
has signed the cheque in question  on behalf of accused
No.1  company  as  its  directors/authorized  signatory.
Accused Nos.2 and 4 are also promoters of the accused
No.1 company. Further, accused Nos.2 to 4 are incharge of
and in active control and management of the accused No.1,
company and responsible to the accused No.1 company for
2

--- Page 49 ---
conducting its business. Further, the accused Nos.2 to 4

3. That the complainant is in the business of iron and

4.  That the complainant has maintained a mutual open

accounts has been maintained detailing the purchase of
goods/items by the accused the persons, the goods/items
supplied to the accused persons, the on account payments
received  by  the  complainant  against  the  goods/items
supplied to the accused persons, interest on delayed

5. That as per the statement of accounts there is an
outstanding amount of Rs.17,04,157/- due the against

6. That towards the aforesaid outstanding amount of
Rs.17,04,157/- the accused persons (as on account part

3

--- Page 50 ---
drawn on Punjab National Bank, Mid Corporate Br., Sector-
17B, Chandigarh, 160017.
7.  That to the utter surprise of the complainant, when
the aforesaid cheque bearing No.161702 for Rs.14,00,000/-

its directors/authorized signatory. Accused Nos.2 and 4
are also promoters of accused No.1 company. Further,
accused Nos.2 to 4 are incharge of and in active control
and  management  of  the  accused  No.1  company  and
responsible to the accused No.1 company for conducting
its business. Further, the accused Nos.2 to 4 have played
full role in the transactions and in purchase of the

Nos.2 to 4 with the common intention had taken conscious
and collective decision to bear all the liabilities
arising out of the goods/items supplied and also towards

liabilities arising out of the cheque in question. In

10. That in consonance with the provisions of Section 138

13. That the present complaint has been filed within the

14. That the registered office of the complainant is in

the reason "Account Closed" vide return memos of Axis

legal notice issued from New Delhi. Hence, this Hon'ble
Court  has  the  jurisdiction  entertain  the  present
complaint.”
[Emphasis supplied]
6. Thus, on plain reading of the complaint, it appears that
there was a business transaction between the appellant-
complainant and the accused no. 1-company for purchase of
goods/items of iron and steel. The cheque amount is to the
5

--- Page 52 ---
tune of Rs.14,00,000/-.
7. According to the complainant, the cheque in question was
a post-dated cheque dated 15.04.2014 drawn on Punjab National
Bank, Mid Corporate Branch, Sector 17-B, Chandigarh, duly
signed by the respondent no. 1/Kuljinder Singh. The cheque in
question came to be dishonoured with an endorsement “Account
Closed”.
8. The appellant-complainant, thereafter, issued statutory
notice under Section 138 of the NI Act and called upon the
accused persons to make good the payment within a period of
15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. Since the
accused  persons  failed  to  make  good  the  payment,  the
appellant  went  before  the  Court  and  lodged  a  private
complaint.
9. It appears that cognizance was taken upon the complaint
lodged by the appellant and process was issued only against
accused no. 1-company and accused no. 2/Kuljinder Singh, but
not against the accused no. 3/Yadvinder Singh or the accused
no. 4/Ajit Singh.
10. Thereafter, the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh preferred a
petition before the High Court, praying for quashing of the
proceedings, essentially on the ground that he had resigned
as the Director of the company on 25.06.2012 and, therefore,
on the date of the commission of the alleged offence, i.e.,
the date when the accused persons are alleged to have failed
6

--- Page 53 ---
to make the payment within 15 days from the date of receipt
of notice, he had nothing to do with the company and,
therefore, would not be liable for the alleged offence.
11. The High Court accepted this submission canvassed by the
accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh and quashed the summoning order
dated  21.03.2015,  qua  the  accused  no.2/Kuljinder  Singh.
However, with respect to accused no. 3/Yadvinder Singh and
accused no. 4/Ajit Singh (deceased), the High Court set aside
the summoning order dated 21.03.2015 and remanded the matter
to the Trial Court, with a direction to consider the same
afresh  with  respect  to  the  liability  of  accused
no.3/Yadvinder Singh and accused no.4/Ajit Singh (deceased).
The  appellant-complainant,  being  dissatisfied  with  the
impugned order passed by the High Court is here before us.
12. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant-
complainant would submit that the High Court committed an
egregious error in passing the impugned order, quashing the
proceedings qua the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh on the
assumption that on the date of the commission of the alleged
offence under Section 138 of the NI Act, the respondent
no.1/accused  no.2/Kuljinder  Singh  had  ceased  to  be  the
Director of the company and could not be held liable for the
dishonour of the cheque. He would submit that there is
nothing  on  record  to  indicate  that  the  respondent
no.1/accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh had resigned from the post
of Director much prior to the presentation of the cheque and
7

--- Page 54 ---
the dishonour of the same.
13. In such circumstances referred to above, the learned
counsel appearing for the appellant-complainant would pray
that there being merit in his appeal, the same be allowed and
the impugned order be set-aside with respect to its decision
qua the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh.
14. We take notice of para 6 of the impugned order. Para 6
reads thus:-
“6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and
after perusing the record with their able assistance, it
transpires that the disputed cheque was issued under the
signature of the petitioner, who was the Director and the
Authorised Signatory at the time. However, the petitioner
had  resigned  from  the  said  post  on  25.06.2012  and
Yadvinder Singh was appointed as his successor.”
15. According to the High Court, as reflected from para 6
referred to above, the cheque in question was issued under
the signature of the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh. This fact
is  not  disputed  even  by  the  respondent  no.1/accused
no.2/Kuljinder Singh.
16. The High Court proceeds on the footing that the accused
no.2/Kuljinder Singh had signed the cheque. The High Court
also proceeds on the footing that the accused no.2/Kuljinder
Singh was the Director and Authorized Signatory. However,
according to the High Court, since the accused no.2/Kuljinder
Singh had resigned from the said post on 25.06.2012 and the
accused no.3/Yadvinder Singh was appointed as his successor,
8

--- Page 55 ---
putting the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh to trial would be an
abuse of the process of law.
17. We are not in agreement with the line of reasoning
adopted by the High Court for the purpose of quashing the
criminal  proceedings  against  the  accused  no.2/Kuljinder
Singh.
18. In this regard, it would be apposite to refer to the
principles enunciated by this Court in  S.P. Mani & Mohan
Dairy v. Snehalatha Elangovan, (2023) 10 SCC 685:
"47.  At  this  stage,  we  should  look  into  the
decision of this Court in K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Vora
[K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Vora, (2009) 10 SCC 48 : (2009)
4 SCC (Civ) 1 : (2010) 2 SCC (Cri) 1181] , wherein
this Court discussed the principles of vicarious
liability of the officers of a company in respect
of dishonour of a cheque and held : (SCC pp. 61-62,
para 27)
“27. The position under Section 141 of the Act
can be summarised thus:
(i)  If  the  accused  is  the  Managing
Director or a Joint Managing Director, it
is not necessary to make an averment in
the complaint that he is in charge of,
and is responsible to the company, for
the  conduct  of  the  business  of  the
company. It is sufficient if an averment
is made that the accused was the Managing
Director or Joint Managing Director at
the relevant time. This is because the
prefix “Managing” to the word “Director”
makes it clear that they were in-charge
of and are responsible to the company,
for the conduct of the business of the
9

--- Page 56 ---
company.
(ii) In the case of a Director or an
officer of the company who signed the
cheque on behalf of the company, there is
no need to make a specific averment that
he was in charge of and was responsible
to the company, for the conduct of the
business  of  the  company  or  make  any
specific  allegation  about  consent,
connivance or negligence. The very fact
that the dishonoured cheque was signed by
him on behalf of the company, would give
rise to responsibility under sub-section
(2) of Section 141.
(iii)  In  the  case  of  a  Director,
Secretary  or  Manager  [as  defined  in
Section 2(24) of the Companies Act] or a
person referred to in clauses (e) and (f)
of Section 5 of the Companies Act, an
averment in the complaint that he was in
charge of, and was responsible to the
company, for the conduct of the business
of the company is necessary to bring the
case under Section 141(1) of the Act. No
further averment would be necessary in
the complaint, though some particulars
will be desirable. They can also be made
liable under Section 141(2) by making
necessary averments relating to consent
and  connivance  or  negligence,  in  the
complaint, to bring the matter under that
sub-section.
(iv) Other Officers of a company cannot
be made liable under sub-section (1) of
Section 141. Other officers of a company
can be made liable only under sub-section
(2) of Section 141, by averring in the
complaint their position and duties in
the company and their role in regard to
the issue and dishonour of the cheque,
disclosing  consent,  connivance  or
negligence.”
(emphasis supplied)
10

--- Page 57 ---
48. In a very recent pronouncement in Sunita
Palita v. Panchami Stone Quarry [Sunita Palita
v. Panchami Stone Quarry, (2022) 10 SCC 152 :
(2023) 1 SCC (Civ) 612 : (2023) 1 SCC (Cri)
91] , this Court, after referring to  K.K.
Ahuja [K.K. Ahuja v. V.K. Vora, (2009) 10 SCC
48 : (2009) 4 SCC (Civ) 1 : (2010) 2 SCC (Cri)
1181] referred to above, observed as under :
(Sunita Palita case [Sunita Palita v. Panchami
Stone Quarry, (2022) 10 SCC 152 : (2023) 1 SCC
(Civ) 612 : (2023) 1 SCC (Cri) 91] , SCC pp.
164-65, para 29)
“29. … when the accused is the Managing
Director or a Joint Managing Director of
a company, it is not necessary to make an
averment in the complaint that he is in
charge of, and is responsible to the
company for the conduct of the business
of  the  company.  This  is  because  the
prefix “Managing” to the word “Director”
makes it clear that the Director was in
charge of and responsible to the company,
for the conduct of the business of the
company. A Director or an officer of the
company who signed the cheque renders
himself  liable  in  case  of  dishonour.
Other officers of a company can be made
liable  only  under  sub-section  (2)  of
Section 141 of the NI Act by averring in
the complaint, their position and duties,
in the company, and their role in regard
to the issue and dishonour of the cheque,
disclosing  consent,  connivance  or
negligence.”
49. In yet one another recent pronouncement in
Ashutosh  Ashok  Parasrampuriya  v.  Gharrkul
Industries  (P)  Ltd.  [ Ashutosh  Ashok
11

--- Page 58 ---
Parasrampuriya v.  Gharrkul  Industries  (P)
Ltd., (2023) 14 SCC 770 : 2021 SCC OnLine SC
915] , this Court after due consideration of
the  decisions  in  S.M.S.  Pharmaceuticals
[S.M.S. Pharmaceuticals Ltd.  v. Neeta Bhalla,
(2005) 8 SCC 89 : 2005 SCC (Cri) 1975] ; S.K.
Alagh v. State of U.P. [S.K. Alagh v. State of
U.P., (2008) 5 SCC 662 : (2008) 2 SCC (Cri)
686]  ;  Maharashtra  State  Electricity
Distribution Co. Ltd. v. Datar Switchgear Ltd.
[Maharashtra  State  Electricity  Distribution
Co. Ltd. v. Datar Switchgear Ltd. , (2010) 10
SCC 479 : (2011) 1 SCC (Cri) 68] , and GHCL
Employees Stock Option Trust v. India Infoline
Ltd. [ GHCL Employees Stock Option Trust  v.
India Infoline Ltd., (2013) 4 SCC 505 : (2013)
2  SCC  (Cri)  414]  ,  observed  as  under  :
(Ashutosh Ashok Parasrampuriya case  [Ashutosh
Ashok Parasrampuriya  v.  Gharrkul Industries
(P) Ltd., (2023) 14 SCC 770 : 2021 SCC OnLine
SC 915] , SCC para 24)
“24. In the light of the ratio in  S.M.S.
Pharmaceuticals  [S.M.S.  Pharmaceuticals
Ltd. v. Neeta Bhalla, (2005) 8 SCC 89 :
2005 SCC (Cri) 1975] and later judgments
of which a reference has been made what
is to be looked into is whether in the
complaint, in addition to asserting that
the appellants are the Directors of the
Company and they are in-charge of and
responsible  to  the  Company  for  the
conduct of the business of the Company
and if statutory compliance of Section
141 of the NI Act has been made, it may
not  be  open  for  the  High  Court  to
interfere under Section 482CrPC unless it
comes  across  some  unimpeachable,
incontrovertible evidence which is beyond
12

--- Page 59 ---
suspicion or doubt or totally acceptable
circumstances which may clearly indicate
that the Director could not have been
concerned with the issuance of cheques
and asking him to stand the trial would
be abused of process of court. Despite
the presence of basic averment, it may
come to a conclusion that no case is made
out against the particular Director for
which there could be various reasons.”
(emphasis supplied)
50.  The  principles  discernible  from  the
aforesaid decision of this Court in Ashutosh
Ashok  Parasrampuriya  [ Ashutosh  Ashok
Parasrampuriya v.  Gharrkul  Industries  (P)
Ltd., (2023) 14 SCC 770 : 2021 SCC OnLine SC
915]  are  that  the  High  Court  should  not
interfere under Section 482 of the Code at the
instance of an accused unless it comes across
some  unimpeachable  and  incontrovertible
evidence to indicate that the Director/partner
of a firm could not have been concerned with
the issuance of cheques. This Court clarified
that in a given case despite the presence of
basic averments, the High Court may conclude
that  no  case  is  made  out  against  the
particular  Director/partner  provided  the
Director/partner  is  able  to  adduce  some
unimpeachable  and  incontrovertible  evidence
beyond suspicion and doubt."
13

--- Page 60 ---
19. In the present case, the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh’s
involvement in the issuance of the cheque is not founded
merely upon his designation as a Director or upon a general
averment made in the complaint. His signature on the cheque,
which is not disputed, constitutes a specific and material
circumstance attracting the aforesaid principles. The High
Court,  however,  proceeded  to  quash  the  proceedings
essentially on the ground that the accused no.2/Kuljinder
Singh had resigned from the directorship on 25.06.2012 and
that another person had thereafter been appointed in his
place. In our considered view, an assertion that the accused
no.2/Kuljinder Singh had resigned prior to the incidence of
dishonour  of  the  cheque,  would  not,  by  itself,  be  a
sufficient basis for quashing the proceedings, particularly
when the cheque had admittedly been signed by him during the
subsistence of his directorship.
20.  It is in this context that the observations made by this
Court in S.P. Mani (Supra) assume significance. This Court
has clarified that, even where the requisite averments are
present, the High Court may exercise its jurisdiction under
Section 482 of the Code only if the accused is able to place
on record unimpeachable and incontrovertible material, beyond
suspicion or doubt, demonstrating that he could not have been
concerned with the issuance of the cheque and that requiring
him to face trial would amount to an abuse of the process of
the Court. In the present case, however, the High Court does
14

--- Page 61 ---
not appear to have found any such material warranting the
exercise of its inherent jurisdiction. On the contrary,
particularly when the factum of the accused no.2/Kuljinder
Singh’s signature on the cheque remains undisputed, the mere
assertion of resignation cannot be treated as sufficient to
conclusively absolve him of the consequences flowing from the
issuance of the cheque at the stage of quashing under Section
482.
21. Thus, the merits of the case, including questions of
fact with respect to issuance of the cheque, resignation by
the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh, the subsequent dishonour of
the cheque, and any liability arising thereof, are questions
best left to be adjudicated at the stage of trial.
22. The liability of the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh for
the offence punishable under Section 138 could have been
determined  only  after  the  complainant  would  have  been
permitted to lead adequate evidence in the course of the
trial.
23. The accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh would, of course, be at
liberty to establish his defence by placing the relevant
material before the competent Court. However, in the absence
of unimpeachable and incontrovertible material which would
justify termination of the proceedings at the threshold, the
High Court ought not to have undertaken an examination of the
accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh’s defence so as to pre-empt the
15

--- Page 62 ---
trial. The correctness of the accused no.2/Kuljinder Singh’s
defence, as also the ultimate question of his liability,
ought to have been left open for determination on the basis
of the evidence led by the parties at trial.
24. In view of the aforesaid, these appeals succeed and are
hereby allowed. The impugned order passed by the High Court
is set-aside to the limited extent that it quashes the
summoning order dated 21.03.2015. The concerned Trial Court
shall now proceed further with the matter, in accordance with
law.
25. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO(S).            OF 2026 
(Arising out of SLP (Civil) No (s). 10745 of 2026)
SANJAY KUMAR 
SAMANTARAY       ….APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
SHANTILATA KHUNTIA
AND OTHERS                     ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  instant  appeal  with  special  leave  is
preferred against the judgment and order dated 18 th
February, 2026 passed by the Division Bench of the
1

--- Page 82 ---
High Court of Orissa at Cuttack 1 in W.P. (C) No.
29658 of 2025.
4. The matter pertains to a tender floated by the
Chief  Engineer  &  Basin  Manager,  Mahanadi
Kathajodi System, Bhubaneswar for e-procurement
vide notice dated 5 th May, 2025 for the work titled
as  “Protection  to  scoured  bank  of  Devi  right
embankment near village Erancha from RD 5.200km
to  RD  7.500  km  (Construction  of  8nos  of  Spurs)”
valued at Rs.26,37,28,875.00/- (Rupees Twenty-Six
Crores Thirty-Seven Lakhs Twenty-Eight Thousand
Eight Hundred and Seventy-Five only). The tender
notice  envisaged  a  two-stage  process  comprising
technical  evaluation  (Cover-I)  and  the  opening  of
final bids (Cover-II) of technically qualified bidders,
with a stipulation under Clause 35 of the Detailed
Tender  Call  Notice2 that  in  the  event  of  multiple
bidders  quoting  an  identical  rate,  the  successful
bidder  was  to  be  selected  through  a  transparent
automated lottery.
5. On  13th August,  2025,  the  Project  Level
Technical  Committee evaluated 16 technical bids,
1  Hereinafter, referred to as “High Court”. 
2  For short, “DTCN”.
2

--- Page 83 ---
and  found  13  bidders,  including  the  appellant,
Sanjay  Kumar  Samantaray,  technically  qualified,
whereas, respondent No.1, Shantilata Khuntia (writ
petitioner  before the High Court) 3, and  two other
bidders were disqualified for non-compliance with
the  technical  eligibility  criteria.  To  be  specific,
respondent  No.1-writ  petitioner  failed  to  furnish
mandatory  “work-in-hand”  details  under  Clause
4(E) of Section 2 of the DTCN required to determine
her bid capacity. 
6. On  18th September,  2025,  the  Procurement
Committee at the Engineer-in-Chief level scrutinized
and approved the recommendations of the Project
Level Technical Committee. Subsequently, on 24 th
September,  2025,  the  Tender  Committee-cum-
Empowered Committee, headed by the Development
Commissioner-cum-Additional  Chief  Secretary,
Department  of  Water  Resources,  Government  of
Odisha confirmed the recommendations and upheld
the  disqualification  of  respondent  No.1-writ
petitioner.
3  Hereinafter, referred to as “respondent No.1-writ 
petitioner”.  
3

--- Page 84 ---
7. On  10th October,  2025,  the  decision  of  the
Tender Committee-cum-Empowered Committee was
formally  communicated  vide  Letter  No.28470,
permitting the authorities to proceed with opening
of  the  financial  bids.  However,  it  is  averred  that
owing to a technical glitch on 13 th October, 2025 at
3:30  PM,  an  incorrect  version  of  the  evaluation
document  was  inadvertently  uploaded  on  the  e-
procurement  portal,  describing  the  reason  for
respondent No.1-writ petitioner’s disqualification as
non-execution of “moorum/sand filling work”.
8. To rectify this inadvertent error, the tendering
authorities  exercised the  portal’s technical  revoke
option at 6:45 PM on the same day, to undo the
incorrect  document  uploaded  and  reverted  the
tender status to the “Technical Bid Opening” stage.
Although, respondent No.1-writ petitioner received
automated  system  emails  at  7:04  PM  (intimating
tender  revocation)  and  at  7:27  PM  (stating  her
technical bid was opened/admitted), the approved
and  corrected  Evaluation  Document  was  duly
uploaded on  the  portal at 7:34 PM on  the  same
evening,  completely  rectifying  the  error  and  re-
4

--- Page 85 ---
affirming  rejection  of  respondent  No.1-writ
petitioner’s  bid, under Clause 4(E) of Section 2 of
the  DTCN,  simultaneously  declaring  13  bidders
technically responsive.
9.  Thus, although there were certain inadvertent
glitches in the communication of these decisions,
the final bids of all 13 technically qualified bidders,
including the appellant, were eventually opened on
14th October, 2025. All 13 bidders were found to
have quoted an identical rate of 14.99% below the
estimated  cost,  thereby  jointly  occupying  the  L-1
position.  Consequently,  an  automatic  lottery  was
conducted in accordance with the tender conditions.
The appellant has set up a specific case that he
emerged successful in the lottery and was declared
as a successful L-1 bidder. The case so set up by
the appellant remains uncontroverted.
10. Parallelly, respondent No.1 instituted W.P.(C)
No. 29658 of 2025 before the High Court on 15 th
October, 2025 challenging the opening of the final
bids  contending  that  once  the  tender  had  been
revoked on 13 th October, the authorities could not
have proceeded further with the process. The High
5

--- Page 86 ---
Court stayed the tender process by order dated 24 th
October, 2025.
11. The appellant has set up a specific case that in
spite of being declared a successful bidder pursuant
to the lottery, he was not impleaded as a party to
the writ petition. This fact is fortified by copy of the
writ petition annexed with the appeal as Annexure
P-14  wherein,  in  the  array  of  parties,  only  the
official  State  authorities  had  been  impleaded  as
respondents. 
12. Upon learning of the said proceedings in the
High Court, the appellant filed I.A. No. 3047 of 2026
seeking  intervention  in  the  writ  petition  on  the
ground that he possessed a direct, substantial and
legally  protectable  interest  in  the  subject  matter,
having emerged as the successful L-1 bidder in the
evaluation process followed by the lottery.
13. However,  without  effectively  adjudicating  or
considering the appellant’s intervention application,
the High Court proceeded to allow the writ petition
vide judgment and order dated 18 th February, 2026,
which is subject matter of challenge in this appeal
6

--- Page 87 ---
preferred by the appellant being the successful L-1
bidder.
14. By  the  impugned  order,  the  High  Court
quashed  the  tender  process  from  the  stage  of
financial  bid  opening  and  directed  the  State
authorities to undertake a fresh technical evaluation
of all bids, including the bid of respondent No.1-writ
petitioner.
15. We  have  heard  and  considered  the
submissions advanced by learned counsel appearing
on behalf of the parties and have gone through the
material placed on record.
16. A  very  relevant  fact  which  needs  to  be
mentioned is that respondent Nos. 2-4, being the
State of Odisha and its authorities, filed a counter
affidavit  dated  22nd September,  2026,  and  have
categorically stated that in compliance of the order
dated  18th February,  2026,  passed  by  the  High
Court, administrative steps were taken and a fresh
technical evaluation of bids was conducted. Upon
such fresh scrutiny, respondent No.1-writ petitioner
has once again failed to satisfy the technical criteria,
as  duly  recorded  in  official  Letter  No.  5798/WE
7

--- Page 88 ---
dated 21 st February, 2026 (Annexure  R-2), which
explicitly  records  that  “the  original  technical  bid
evaluation  shall  remain  unchanged  even  after  re-
evaluation”. The fact regarding the appellant having
succeeded in the automated lottery process as L-1
bidder is also not in dispute.
17. In this background, we are fully satisfied that
the  interference  made  by  the  High  Court  in  the
tender  process,  which  was  initiated  for  a  very
crucial work for protecting the embankment of Devi
River,  was  not  justified.  The  fact  remains  that
technical bid of respondent No.1-writ petitioner had
been  rejected  upon  evaluation,  which  status
remains  unaltered  even  after  re-evaluation,  as  is
stated  in  the  letter  dated  21st February,  2026
(supra). 
18. Notably,  respondent  No.1-writ  petitioner  has
not countered the said assertion made in the said
letter.  We  may  note  that  despite  due  service  of
notice, respondent No.1 has chosen not to appear
before this Court to contest the proceedings.
19. It  is  true  that  initially  certain  inadvertent
typographical  errors  occurred  in  recording  the
8

--- Page 89 ---
reasons for disqualification of respondent No.1-writ
petitioner  but those inadvertent errors have been
duly rectified and explained by the respondents in
their pleadings before the High Court and so also
before this Court. The respondent No.1, being the
writ petitioner before the High Court, also failed to
implead the appellant (successful bidder) as a party
respondent  before  the  High  Court  and  hence,
evidently, the impugned order suffers from the vice,
having  been  passed  behind  the  back  of  the
successful  bidder  i.e.,  the  appellant  herein  and
cannot be sustained. It is noteworthy that there was
no  allegation  of  mala fide in  the  bid  evaluation
process undertaken by the respondent authorities.
20. While  we  would  have  ordinarily  considered
remanding the matter to the High Court for fresh
adjudication but keeping in view the fact that the
tender  was  issued  for  a  very  crucial  work,  i.e.,
“Protection to scoured bank of Devi right embankment
near village Erancha from RD 5.200km to RD 7.500
km  (Construction  of  8nos  of  Spurs)”  and  as
respondent  No.1-writ  petitioner  has  remained
unresponsive on the technical aspect even after re-
9

--- Page 90 ---
evaluation, no useful purpose would be served by
remanding the matter to the High Court for fresh
consideration. Accordingly, the impugned order is
set aside.
21. The  appellant,  who  had  succeeded  in  the
tender  process  and  had  been  picked  out  as  the
successful L-1 bidder through the automated lottery
process,  shall  be  issued  the  work  order  at  the
earliest and not later than four weeks from the date
of submission of a certified copy of this order before
the competent authority.
22. The appeal is allowed in these terms. No order
as to costs.
23. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. IA No.167477/2026 (application for intervention) is allowed.
The applicant(s) is permitted to intervene in the matter.
2. With  reference  to  the  various  suggestions  made  and
consequential directions proposed by the learned Amicus Curiae in
her Note dated 14.10.2026, the learned Attorney General for India
has placed on record a Note dated 28.10.2026, suggesting certain
directions on behalf of the Union of India.
3. While we are inclined to issue appropriate directions, having
regard to the suggestions made by the learned Amicus Curiae as well
as the Union of India, we consider it appropriate, in the first
instance, to examine the Reserve Bank of India (Know Your Customer)
Amendment Directions, 2026, which are proposed to be notified by
30.11.2026 and operationalized by 31.12.2026.
4. We  reiterate  and  emphasize  that  the  regulatory  measures
proposed by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) must mandate and
incorporate suitable provisions that require financial institutions
to indemnify victims of digital arrest scams and other cyber frauds
and pay suitable compensation not less than the amount lost by the
customer, where it is established that the fraud or crime occurred
due to the failure on the part of the financial institution to
exercise due diligence in preventing or reporting the act/incident.
5. We  have  also  emphasised  in  the  past  various  preventive
safeguards that must be mandated for every financial institution.
12

--- Page 106 ---
These may include  temporarily suspending unusual or suspicious
transactions  inconsistent  with  the  account's  past  transaction
history, automatically intimating such transactions to the nearest
police station, and subsequently physically verifying the reported
transactions to ascertain their genuineness.
6. In order to ensure effective implementation of the regulatory
measures proposed by the RBI, as well as the directions issued by
us, we further direct the RBI to submit a list of all the
authorized financial institutions before this court on the next
date of hearing.
7. Meanwhile, we also direct all the Law Enforcement Agencies in
States and Union Territories to submit the status of the FIRs
registered thus far in connection with digital arrest scam cases
and the resultant investigation undertaken. They shall also suggest
appropriate measures for the prevention, detection and prosecution
of such cases. The Directors General of Police of all States and
Union Territories shall ensure compliance with these directions.
The information furnished to this Court shall simultaneously be
forwarded to the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C).
8. WhatsApp  LLC  (A  Meta  Company)  and  other  concerned
intermediaries are also directed to apprise this Court of the
measures they propose to undertake to prevent the digital arrest
scams and related cybercrimes. They shall also simultaneously
submit their proposals to the I4C.
9. Post this matter for further consideration on 23.11.2026.
(NITIN TALREJA)                            (PREETHI DILEEP KUMAR)
ASTT. REGISTRAR-cum-PS                        DY. REGISTRAR

--- Page 109 ---
3
totality of circumstances has been submitted, but

8. The Special Leave Petition (Criminal) No.
5485/2024 was filed challenging the order dated

10. Thereafter,  on  17.03.2026,  Hubtown  filed

under the said State Money Lending Laws,

--- Page 111 ---
5
shall be considered and adjudicated by the
competent  courts  on  their  own  merits,

12. Vide order dated 06.04.2026, the prayer has
been  accepted,  leading  to  the  filing  of  an
application  at  the  instance  of  Hubtown.
Accordingly, Ashok Commercial Enterprises has filed
the present M.A. D. No. 41896/2026 for impleadment
and recall of the Order dated 06.04.2026.
13. Mr.  Shyam  Divan  argues  that  the
clarification in M.A. No. 1176/2026 does not align
with the established procedure in either three-tier
or  four-tier  litigation.  Hubtown  has  been
unsuccessful in a few of its efforts in CS No. 1532
of 2018, a suit pending between the parties for the
recovery of an amount.
14. Hubtown, aggrieved by the adverse Orders in
the Applications filed by Hubtown, has pursued
remedies before this Court. The outcome of those
remedies need not be adverted to. However, the
point  he  makes  is  that,  by  referring  to  the
clarification dated 06.04.2026, a fresh set of
applications to non-suit the plaintiff has been
initiated.  Therefore,  it  is  argued  that  the
declaration in the clarification application that
it will not affect a party or is innocuous in

--- Page 112 ---
6
nature is a subterfuge. The plaintiff in CS No.
1532 of 2018 and the applicant in the present
application  are  prejudiced  by  the  order  dated
06.04.2026. Therefore, on the short ground that,
behind the back of Ashok Commercial Enterprises,
the order has been obtained without going into the
merits  and  that  the  same  is  contrary  to  the
judgments of this Court, some of which are as
follows:
A. Budhia Swain v. Gopinath Deb (1999) 4 SCC 396: A
tribunal or a court may recall an order earlier
made by it if( i) the proceedings culminating in an
order suffer from an inherent lack of jurisdiction
and such lack of jurisdiction is patent;( ii) there
exists  fraud  or  collusion  in  obtaining  the
judgment;(iii) there has been a mistake of the
court prejudicing a party, or( iv) a judgment was
rendered in ignorance of the fact that a necessary
party had not been served at all or had died and
the estate was not represented. 
B. Indian Bank v. Satyam Fibres (India) (P) Ltd.,
(1996) 5 SCC 550 :  The judiciary also possesses
inherent power, especially under Section 151 CPC,
to recall its judgment or order if it is obtained
by fraud on the court. This power is necessary for
the orderly administration of the court's business.
Since fraud affects the solemnity, regularity, and

--- Page 113 ---
7
orderliness of the court's proceedings and amounts
to an abuse of the process of the court, courts
have been held to have inherent power to set aside
an order obtained by fraud practised upon that
court. Similarly, where a party misleads the court
or  the  court  itself  commits  a  mistake  that
prejudices a party, the court has inherent power to
recall its order.
C. Ghanashyam Mishra and Sons (P) Ltd. v. Edelweiss
Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd., (2024) 19 SCC 374 :
There is a growing tendency to indirectly seek
review  of  this  Court's  orders  by  filing
applications seeking modification or clarification
of  the  orders  passed  by  this  Court.  Such
applications are a total abuse of the process of
law. The Court spends valuable time deciding such
applications, time that would otherwise be utilised
to attend to the litigations of litigants who have
waited in the corridors of justice for decades.
15. Mr.  Amit  Rawal,  learned  senior  counsel
appearing  for  the  respondent,  argues  that  the
applicant in M.A. No. 1176/2026 sought only limited
clarification and that the pending applications are
expected to be heard and disposed of in accordance
with law.
16. On  the  first  principle,  whether  Ashok
Commercial Enterprises is a proper and necessary

--- Page 114 ---
8
party to M.A. No. 1176/2026, we are of the view
that, in light of the Respondent's prayer for
amendment, Ashok Commercial Enterprises is both a
proper and a necessary party.
17. We may hasten to add that M.A. No. 1176/2026
again is not in line with the circular issued by
the Supreme Court of India on 03.01.2025. We prefer
not  to  go  into  further  detail  on  all  the
circumstances we have noted, but it suffices to
observe that the order dated 06.04.2026 has been
obtained  or  passed  behind  the  back  of  Ashok
Commercial Enterprises, the plaintiff in CS No.
1532  of  2018,  where  Hubtown  is  one  of  the
defendants.
18. The parties have issues in the pending CS
No. 1532 of 2018; therefore, we are of the view

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
  CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________OF 2026 
(@ SLP(Criminal) No.13108/2026)
VISHWAJEET SINGH @BISHWAJEET 
RAMANAND             APPELLANT(S)
                             VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR & ORS.         RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal arises from the order passed by the
High Court of Judicature at Patna dated 01.07.2026 in
Criminal Miscellaneous No.74033 of 2025 by which the
Criminal Miscellaneous Application preferred by the
respondent no.2-the de facto-complainant, praying for
cancellation of regular bail granted to the appellant
before us, came to be allowed, and thereby the
appellant was asked to be taken in custody.
1

--- Page 119 ---
3. It appears from the materials on record that a
First Information Report came to be lodged with the
Vigilance Police Station bearing Case No. 29 of 2025,
against the appellant for the offence punishable
under Section 7(b) of the Prevention of Corruption
Act, 1988 (for short, “the Act, 1988”).
4. The  materials  on  record  indicate  that  the
appellant is serving as a Manager/Administrator in a
Hospital by name Sadar Hospital, Samastipur.  This
hospital appears to be a Government Hospital.  The
allegations  against  the  appellant  are  that  he
demanded a bribe of the amount of Rs.4,000/- for the
purpose  of  clearing  the  wages  of  the  de  facto
complainant to the tune of Rs.36,421/-.
5. In connection with the FIR referred to above, the
appellant came to be arrested. Later he was ordered
to be released on bail by the Sessions Court.
6. The de facto complainant, being dissatisfied with
the order passed by the Sessions Court releasing the
2

--- Page 120 ---
appellant on bail, challenged the same before the
High Court.  The High Court thought fit to interfere
with the order passed by the Sessions Court and
accordingly  cancelled  the  bail  granted  to  the
appellant.
7. In  such  circumstances,  the  appellant  is  here
before us with the present appeal.
8. We heard Mr. Awanish Sinha, the learned counsel
appearing for the appellant, Mr. Karan Verma, the
learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  de  facto
complainant (respondent no.2), Ms. Aditi Tripathi,
the learned counsel appearing for the State and Mr.
Parth Shekhar, the learned counsel appearing for the
respondent no. 4, respectively.
9. We take notice of the fact that after a period of
almost one year from the date of release of the
appellant on bail by the Sessions Court, the High
Court thought fit to disturb the order and cancel the
bail.
3

--- Page 121 ---
10.Prima facie , it appears from the tenor of the
impugned order that what weighed with the High Court
was the observation of the Sessions Court, while
releasing the appellant on bail that the bribe amount
was paltry.
11.Ordinarily, in cases of this type, having regard
to the maximum punishment that the trial court would
impose, ultimately, if the accused is held to be
guilty, bail is to be granted. It is only when there
are criminal antecedents or the facts are very gross
that the court may decline to exercise its discretion
in favour of the accused.
12.The High Court may be right in observing that the
quantum of the bribe amount is not a relevant factor
for the purpose of determining whether bail should be
granted or not. However,  High  Court  could  have
observed this much and allowed the appellant accused
to remain on bail.
13.In such circumstances, referred to above, we are
4

--- Page 122 ---
of the view that we should set aside the impugned
order passed by the High Court and restore the
original bail order passed by the Sessions Court. We
order accordingly.
14.However, there is one disturbing feature which we
should not ignore.  It appears, that upon arrest, the
appellant accused was in judicial custody for almost
a period of 15 days.  Once a public servant is
arrested and remains in judicial custody for more
than 48 hours, there is a deemed suspension. He being
a public servant, he could be said to have been
placed under deemed suspension.  No specific order is
required to be passed in this regard.
15.We are informed by the learned counsel appearing
for the State that in fact the appellant was placed
under suspension but later, the suspension order came
to be revoked, and, shockingly, he has been once
again posted in the very same hospital and that too
on the very same post. This aspect shall be looked
5

--- Page 123 ---
into by the State at the earliest. 
16.We expect the State to do the needful in the
matter in accordance with law.
17.With the aforesaid, the appeal stands disposed
of.
18.Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

[J.B. PARDIWALA]

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur,
by the impugned order dated 20.03.2026, has rejected
the appellant’s prayer for bail.
3. Appellant, is figuring as an accused in FIR
No.246 of 2024, registered at Police Station Bichhua,
District Chhindwara, Madhya Pradesh, under Sections
103(1), 115(2), 351(3) and 3(5) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya  Sanhita,  2023  and  Section  3(2)(v)  of  the
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of
Atrocities) Act, 1989.
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
1

--- Page 142 ---
the incident arose out of a sudden fight without any
premeditation, wherein the appellant along with other
persons allegedly assaulted the deceased, and the
allegation against the appellant is that he used a
knife. It is further submitted that the appellant has
been in custody since 27.07.2024.  It is further
brought to the notice of this Court that all the
other co-accused persons have already been enlarged
on bail.
5. The aforesaid fact regarding grant of bail to
the co-accused persons has not been disputed by the
learned counsel for the respondent-State, though he
points out that a knife was recovered at instance of
the petitioner.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties
and  taking  into  consideration  the  documents  on
record, the period of incarceration undergone by the
appellant, as well as the fact that all other co-
accused persons have already been granted bail, this
Court is of the opinion that the appellant also
deserves to be enlarged on bail.
2

--- Page 143 ---
7. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned order
of the High Court.

the trial court and subject to such other terms and

9. Needless to observe, the appellant shall not,
directly or indirectly, by making inducement, threat
or promise, dissuade any person acquainted with the
facts of the case from disclosing such facts to the
court.

and conditions for grant of bail, the trial court
shall be at liberty to cancel the bail of the
appellant.
11. It is also ordered that the appellant shall
diligently attend proceedings of the trial, unless
exempted. If he is found to abstain from attending

also be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of

3

--- Page 144 ---

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
IA Nos.295594/2026 AND 245496/2026.
1. These two Interlocutory Applications have been filed by accused nos. 1
and 4 for grant of bail and suspension of sentence.
2. The allegations according to the prosecution made against accused nos. 1
and 4 are similar and identical to the one  made against accused nos. 2 and 3
respectively. This Court while examining prayer of accused nos. 2 and 3, vide
orders dated 31.08.2026 and 22.09.2026 passed in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1275-
1276/2024, respectively, has opined as under:-
“2. The applicant – accused No.2 (Yogeesha) came to
be tried for an offence punishable under Sections 143,
148, 302, 201 and 114 read with Section 149 of the
Indian  Penal  Code,  1860  (“IPC”)  in  Sessions  Case
No.216/2012 and acquitted on 23.09.2016 for the said
offences  on  appreciation  of  evidence.  The  appellate
court reversed the said finding and convicted accused
Nos.1 to 4 under Section 304 read with 34 of the IPC,
accused  Nos.5  and  6  under  Section  302  read  with
Sections 114 and 34 of the IPC and accused Nos.1, 2
and 4 under Section 201 of the IPC. The acquittal under
Sections 143 and 148 of the IPC was maintained. The
trial court by its judgment of acquittal had opined that
the evidence of eye-witnesses PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4
was unreliable and the prosecution had failed to prove
satisfactorily the motive and recovery of weapons. The
deficiencies  in  the  eye-witnesses’  statements  also
swayed in the mind of the trial court to acquit them.
The  High  Court  by  the  impugned  judgment  after
re-appreciation of evidence was of the view that the
eye-witnesses’  statements  would  establish  their
    Criminal Appeal  No(s). 1275-1276/2024                                                                2

--- Page 167 ---
presence  at  the  scene  of  crime  and  they  had  also
identified the accused. The fact that there was no T est
Identification  Parade  conducted  seems  to  have  not
been taken into account by the appellate court. As to
the actual motive for the incident which weighed with
the trial court is yet another factor which requires to be
examined  by  this  Court  in  the  light  of  the  finding
arrived  at  by  the  High  Court.  For  these  cumulative
reasons, we are of the considered view that in the light
of  divergent  findings,  the  sentence  imposed  on
appellant  –  applicant  (Yogeesha)  deserves  to  be
suspended and enlarged the applicant – accused No.2
(Yogeesha) on bail.
2. The applicant – accused No.3 (Abdul Nabi @ Chand
Pasha) came to be tried alongwith other accused for an
offence punishable under Sections 143, 148, 302, 201
and  114  read  with  Section  149  of  the  Indian  Penal
Code, 1860 (“IPC”) in Sessions Case No.216/2012 and
acquitted  on  23.09.2016  for  the  said  offences  on
appreciation of evidence. The appellate court reversed
the  said  finding  and  convicted  accused  Nos.1  to  4
under Section 302 read with 34 of the IPC, accused
Nos.5 and 6 under Section 302 read with Sections 114
and 34 of the IPC and accused Nos.1, 2 and 4 under
Section 201 of the IPC. The acquittal under Sections
143 and 148 of the IPC was maintained. The trial court
by  its  judgment  of  acquittal  had  opined  that  the
evidence of eye-witnesses PW-2, PW-3 and PW-4 was
unreliable  and  the  prosecution  had  failed  to  prove
satisfactorily the motive and recovery of weapons. The
deficiencies  in  the  eye-witnesses’  statements  also
swayed in the mind of the trial court to acquit them.
The  High Court by the impugned judgment after re-
appreciation of evidence was of the view that the eye-
    Criminal Appeal  No(s). 1275-1276/2024                                                                3

--- Page 168 ---
witnesses’ statements would establish their presence at
the  scene of crime  and they had also identified the
accused. The fact that there was no T est Identification
Parade conducted seems to have not been taken into
account by the appellate court. 
3. Learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  State  would
oppose the grant of bail by contending that applicant
had sought for grant of bail on earlier occasion and this
Court by order dated 22.08.2024 had rejected the same
and the prayer of accused No.2 (Yogeesha) had never
been  considered  by  this  Court  and  as  such  the
applicant cannot claim parity.
4. A  perusal  of  the  order  dated  22.08.2024  would
indicate that prayer of the present applicant was not
entertained by opining that it was not a case for grant
of suspension of sentence and bail ‘at that stage’. This
Court having taken note of the fact that there was a
reversal of acquittal passed by the trial court into a
conviction by the High Court and the fact that actual
motive for the incident requires to be examined in the
light of divergent views expressed by the Courts, we
are of the considered view that sentence imposed on
the appellant / applicant (Abdul Nabi @ Chand Pasha –
A-3)  deserves  to  be  suspended  and  he  should  be
released on bail. Accordingly, the application is allowed.
The sentence imposed on the applicant – accused No.3
(Abdul  Nabi  @  Chand  Pasha)  stands  suspended  and
applicant – accused No.3 (Abdul Nabi @ Chand Pasha)
is ordered to be enlarged on bail by the jurisdictional
Sessions  Court  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  it
deems fit to impose.”
    Criminal Appeal  No(s). 1275-1276/2024                                                                4

--- Page 169 ---
3. Insofar  as  accused  no.  5  is  concerned,  this  Court  by  order  dated
19.12.2025 has released him on bail by suspending the sentence after opining
as under:-
3) After hearing learned counsel and on perusal of the
record, we find that the role of the appellant-accused
No.5(Yadukumara)  is  only  of  instigator.  However,
considering  the  aforesaid,  without  expressing  any
opinion  on  the  merits  of  the  case,  we  deem  it
appropriate to suspend the substantive jail sentence of
the appellant-Yadukumara, subject to the final outcome
of  Criminal  Appeal  Nos.3462-  3465  of  2024.  The
appellant-Yadukumara be released on bail on such terms
and conditions as may be deemed fit and imposed by
the trial Court.
4. The learned counsel for the respondent-State of Karnataka vehemently
opposes the grant of bail by contending that on re-appreciation of evidence, the
Appellate  Court  has  come  to  a  conclusion  about  the  complicity  of  the
appellants/applicants herein.
5. Having regard to the fact that accused nos. 1, 3 and 5 having been
released on bail against whom the allegations made are similar and identical to
the allegations made against accused nos. 1 and 4, we are of the considered
view, that appellants/applicants are entitled for similar relief and hence, the
present Interlocutory Applications are hereby allowed and sentence imposed on
the  appellants/applicants  stands  suspended  and  appellants/applicants  are
ordered  to  be  released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional Courts deems fit to impose.

discretionary exercise of the Appellate Authority did
not  suffer  from  non-application  of  mind.   The
discretion to be exercised is in the context of
proviso to Section 15, which provides as under :-
“15.(1) Any  person  aggrieved  by  any
decision or order made by the Adjudicating
Authority  under  this  Act  may  prefer  an
appeal,—
(a) where the decision or order has been
made by the Director General, to the Central
Government;
(b) where the decision or order has been
made  by  an  officer  subordinate  to  the
Director General, to the Director General or
to any officer superior to the Adjudicating
Authority authorised by the Director General
to hear the appeal, 

--- Page 184 ---
2
within a period of forty-five days from the
date on which the decision or order is
served on such person: 
Provided that the Appellate Authority may,
if it is satisfied that the appellant was
prevented  by  sufficient  cause  from
preferring the appeal within the aforesaid
period, allow such appeal to be preferred
within a further period of thirty days: 
Provided further that in the case of an
appeal against a decision or order imposing
a penalty or redemption charges, no such
appeal  shall  be  entertained  unless  the
amount of the penalty or redemption charges
has been deposited by the appellant: 
Provided  also  that,  where  the  Appellate
Authority is of opinion that the deposit to
be made will cause undue hardship to the
appellant,  it  may,  at  its  discretion,
dispense  with  such  deposit  either
unconditionally  or  subject  to  such
conditions as it may impose. 
(2)  The  Appellate  Authority  may,  after
giving  to  the  appellant  a  reasonable
opportunity  of  being  heard,  if  he  So
desires,  and  after  making  such  further
inquiries,  if  any,  as  it  may  consider
necessary, make such orders as it thinks
fit, confirming, modifying or reversing the
decision or order appealed against, or may
send back the case with such directions, as
it may think fit, for a fresh adjudication

--- Page 185 ---
3
or decision, as the case may be, after
taking additional evidence, if necessary:
Provided that an order enhancing or imposing
a  penalty  or  redemption  charges  or
confiscating goods of a greater value shall
not be made under this section unless the
appellant has been given an opportunity of
making  a  representation,  and,  if  hv  so
desires, of being heard in his defence, 
(3)  The  order  made  in  appeal  by  the
Appellate Authority shall be final.”

1
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL  NO.770/2017
  THE STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH                         APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
VIPIN                                              RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the appellant.
Since  none  appeared  for  the  respondent  on  the  earlier
occasion, this Court was pleased to appoint Mr. Nikhil Goel,
learned Senior counsel, as the Amicus Curiae to appear for the
respondent, whom we have also heard. 
2. The occurrence in the instant case was on 06.02.2012. The
complaint has been given by PW-1, who is the father of the
deceased victim, on the next day morning i.e. on 07.02.2012,
for the offence punishable under Sections 302, 376 and 201 of
the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The complaint proceeds to state
that the respondent was seen with the deceased victim and, on
being confronted about the same, it is alleged that he
quarreled with PW-1 and PW-2 and evaded their queries. After

--- Page 189 ---
2
searching for the deceased victim, and upon finding her dead
body, the instant complaint was given. 
3. A total of nine witnesses were examined before the Trial
Court. The Trial Court, by primarily placing reliance upon the
ocular evidence of PWs - 1 to 3, was pleased to render a
conviction. 
4. On an appeal by the respondent, the High Court was pleased to
overturn the conviction on the premise that the conduct of
PWs-1 to 3 raised serious doubts. It was held that there were
no attempts on their part to check with the respondent about
the whereabouts of the deceased victim at the very beginning.
It was further held that the presence of PW-2, who is a close
relative of PW-1, was also highly doubtful, as he was running
a shop in a different place. It was also held that PW-3, being
a child witness, has stated in cross examination that she made
the statement as instructed by her mother. The dead body of
the deceased victim, which was found on 07.02.2012, was lying
on the road from the previous night itself. The person who
informed the police after identifying the dead body has also
not been examined. The DNA test conducted also does not
clearly implicate the respondent.
5. Accordingly, on the aforesaid findings, the High Court was
pleased to extend the benefit of doubt to the respondent and
acquitted him after noting that it is a case of circumstantial

--- Page 190 ---
3
evidence and, therefore, the parameters required are not
satisfied pointing the offence committed to the respondent, by
excluding all other possibilities. Aggrieved, the State of
Uttar Pradesh is before us. 
6. Learned counsel appearing for the appellant – State would
submit  that  the  ocular  evidence  of  PWs  -  1  to  3,
notwithstanding the discrepancies, ought to have been seen by
the High Court as a whole. It is a heinous case of murder
coupled with rape, a fact which is clearly shown by the DNA
report. The fact that the respondent was making an attempt to
flee would also lend credence to the case of the prosecution.
7. Mr. Nikhil Goel, learned Senior counsel appearing as an
Amicus,  submitted  that  there  is  absolutely  no  concrete
material or evidence to implicate the respondent. As stated,
this being a case of circumstantial evidence, the High Court
has rightly rendered an acquittal by disbelieving the evidence
of PWs - 1 to 3 by giving cogent reasoning. Therefore, there
is no need for interference with the impugned order.
8. Having heard the parties, the following are our findings. In a
case of circumstantial evidence, it is a well settled position
of law that the evidence should solely point out to the
accused who has been charged. In other words, in the facts of
the instant case, the circumstances should be such that the
alleged offence could not have been done by anybody else other

--- Page 191 ---
4
than the respondent. Once we disbelieve the evidence of PW-3
who, even as per the prosecution, has admitted in her cross
examination  that  she  was  asked  to  testify  as  per  the
instructions of her mother, there is absolutely no other
evidence available to implicate the appellant. 
9. Once the High Court has found it fit that the benefit of doubt
has  to  be  extended  to  the  respondent  -  accused,  the
presumption  of  innocence  in  his  favour  would  only  get
strengthened.  As  we  find  no  perversity  in  the  ultimate
conclusion of the High Court, the appeal stands dismissed
accordingly. 
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

    IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 14188 OF 2026
(ARISING OUT OF S.L.P. (C) NO. 25728 OF 2026)
THE ANDAMAN & NICOBAR ADMINISTRATION & ORS.   ...APPELLANTS
VERSUS
NAZREEN BANU & ANR.     ...RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal calls in question the impugned
judgment and order dated 19.12.2025 passed by the High
Court  at  Calcutta,  Circuit  Bench  at  Port  Blair  in
MAT/47/2025,  whereby,  the  appeal  preferred  by  the
appellants herein was dismissed, upholding the order dated
27.02.2025  passed  by  the  learned  Single  Judge  in
WPA/653/2024  allowing  the  Writ  Petition  filed  by  the
respondents herein. 
3. Brief facts leading upto filing of the present appeal
are that the respondent No. 2 is the daughter of respondent
No.1-mother who belongs to the Scheduled Tribes Community &
the father does not belong to Scheduled Tribes Community.
The  respondents  had  applied  for  a  Scheduled  Tribes
Certificate and when no response was received from the
1

--- Page 199 ---
authorities, the respondents filed a Writ Petition seeking
grant of Schedule Tribes certificate and a further direction
to the petitioner No.4 to dispose of their application.
4. The  learned  Single  Judge,  in  the  interregnum,
directed the appellant No.4/Tehsildar to dispose of the
application filed by the respondents. Pursuant to this
direction, the Tehsildar rejected the said application. The
learned  Single  Judge  then  quashed  the  said  order  of
rejection and allowed the Writ Petition.  
5. We  have  heard  the  learned  Additional  Solicitor
General  ('ASG')  appearing  for  the  appellants  and  the
learned Senior Counsel appearing for the respondents. 
6. Upon perusal of the impugned judgment, we are of the
view that the High Court has committed an error by taking
the role of the Tehsildar, in determining as to whether the
respondent No.2 belongs to the Scheduled Tribes Community
and are entitled to the benefit of the same. The same was
held on the premise that the respondent No.1-mother belongs
to the Scheduled Tribes Community and that whether the
respondent No.2's upbringing was in an environment which a
member of the Scheduled Tribes Community candidate is
expected to undergo. 
7. The same being a question of fact, the High Court
2

--- Page 200 ---
ought not to have dismissed the writ appeal preferred by
the appellants. 
8. Taking note of the above, we are inclined to set
aside  the  order  passed  by  the  Division  Bench  dated
19.12.2025 in MAT/47/2025 and the order dated 27.02.2025 in
WPA/653/2024, passed by the learned Single Judge of High
Court at Calcutta, Circuit Bench at Port Blair and remit
the matter to the Court of the Tehsildar, Car Nicobar,
Andaman & Nicobar Administration, on the issue pertaining
to the status of the respondent No.2 belonging to the
Scheduled Tribes Community. 
9. Needless to state that the Tehsildar concerned shall
take into consideration the views of the appellants while
deciding the issue before it, apart from hearing the
respondents.
10. The  Tehsildar  concerned  is  directed  to  pass
appropriate orders within a period of three months from the
date of receipt of a copy of this order. 
11. We make it clear that inasmuch as we are remitting
the  matter  back  to  the  Court  of  the  Tehsildar,  the
education being undertaken by respondent No.2, shall not be
affected till the matter is decided, in any manner. 
3

--- Page 201 ---
12. Accordingly,  the  appeal  stands  allowed  in  the
aforesaid terms. 
13. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(arising out of SLP(Crl.) 5142/2026)
SHEETAL KAPOOR ..... APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
PRAVEEN KUMAR & ANR. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Sheetal Kapoor, is the widow of the victim,
Ankush Sharma, who met with an untimely death on 10.08.2024,
leading to the registration of First Information Report (FIR)
No. 0345/2024 dated 22.08.2024 on the file of Police Station –
Beta 2, District – Greater Noida (Commissionerate Gautam Buddha
Nagar), Uttar Pradesh, for offences punishable under Sections
123, 103(1) and 238 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.  
3. Respondent  No.  1  herein,  Praveen  Kumar,  was  arrested  in
connection with the above FIR on 23.08.2024.  Upon completion
of the investigation, a chargesheet was laid against him on
16.11.2024.  His application for grant of bail was dismissed by
the jurisdictional Sessions Court on 13.12.2024. The High Court
of Judicature at Allahabad1 rejected his application in Criminal
Miscellaneous Bail Application No. 5973/2025 for grant of bail,
on 08.09.2025.  However, his second application for grant of
1 “High Court”, for short
Crl.A @ SLP(Crl.) No. 5142/2026  1

--- Page 209 ---
bail in Criminal Miscellaneous Bail Application No. 38480/2025
succeeded, as the High Court deemed it appropriate to allow the
same, vide the impugned order dated 11.11.2025, and granted him
bail subject to conditions.
4. Aggrieved by this turn of events, the appellant, Sheetal
Kapoor, is before this Court, by way of the present appeal.
5. Perusal of the impugned order dated 11.11.2025 reflects that
the High Court was influenced by the fact that only 3 out of
the 30 witnesses listed for examination by the prosecution had
been examined and there was no possibility of early conclusion
of the trial. Significantly, the High Court noted as follows: -
“Considering all those facts and circumstances,
the  nature  of  accusations,  severity  of  the
punishment in the case of conviction and nature of
supporting evidence, reasonable apprehension of
tampering with the witness and prima facie case,
but without commenting on merit of case, a case
for bail is made out.”
6. This Court is at a loss to understand the reasoning of the High
Court, as spelt out in the aforestated paragraph.  Having noted
that  there  was  a  reasonable  apprehension  of  the  accused
tampering with the witnesses, given the fact that he is a
member of the Delhi Police, the High Court seems to have just
brushed it aside along with all other factors that weighed
against him, which it mentioned in detail.
7. Given the nature of the case and the seriousness of the
allegations levelled against respondent No. 1, Praveen Kumar, a
Crl.A @ SLP(Crl.) No. 5142/2026  2

--- Page 210 ---
member of the uniformed service, this was not a deserving and
fit case for the High Court to have shown any indulgence to him
merely because there was no possibility of the trial concluding
soon.
8. We, therefore, hold that the High Court erred in exercising its
discretion in favour of respondent No. 1, Praveen Kumar, at
that stage and in granting him bail in relation to the FIR in
question.
9. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed, setting aside the order
dated  11.11.2025  passed  by  the  High  Court  in  Criminal
Miscellaneous Bail Application No. 38480/2025.  
10. Respondent No. 1 shall surrender within two weeks.  He would,
however, be at liberty to renew his plea upon a change in
circumstances and in accordance with law at an appropriate
stage.
    Pending application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.13859 OF 2026
RAJENDRA TIWARI APPELLANT(S)
                              VERSUS
UNION OF INDIA & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The appellant approached the National Green Tribunal,
Central Zone Bench, Bhopal (“NGT”), by way of O.A. No.
171/2026 (CZ). He challenged the construction of a hotel by
Respondent No. 8, with a built-up area of more than 20,000
sq. m., allegedly within the Nahargarh Wildlife Sanctuary,
Jaipur. It was alleged that the construction was being
carried  out  without  prior  environmental  clearance  and
without wildlife clearance. The appellant relied on the
notification  dated  21.11.1961,  whereby  the  lands  of
Nahargarh were declared forest land, and on the notification
dated 22.09.1980 declaring the Nahargarh Wildlife Sanctuary.
He also relied on the notification dated 08.03.2019, whereby
the  Ministry  of  Environment,  Forest  and  Climate  Change
notified an Eco-Sensitive Zone around the Sanctuary.
1

--- Page 219 ---
2. It  appears  that  the  Forest  Department  thereafter
prepared a revised map of the Sanctuary, so that the actual
area of the reserved forest and the Wildlife Sanctuary could
be identified. That revised map is under challenge before
the High Court of Rajasthan, Bench at Jaipur, in D.B. Civil
Writ Petition (PIL) No. 14254/2025. The pendency of those
proceedings has been noticed by the NGT in paragraph 20 of
the impugned judgment.
3. By the impugned judgment dated 13.08.2026, the NGT has
dismissed  the  Original  Application  as  not  maintainable,
holding, inter alia, that: 
(i) the land is recorded as private property in the revenue
records, and the issues concerning the lease deed, revenue
entries and mutation are not within the domain of the NGT; 
(ii) the identification and demarcation of the Nahargarh
Wildlife Sanctuary is under process. A Committee constituted
by the Principal Chief Conservator of Forests has examined
the  survey  map  and  finalised  the  identification  and
demarcation,  and  the  matter  is  pending  with  the  State
Government; 
(iii) the proceedings concerning the revised map are pending
before the High Court, and unless the boundary of the
Sanctuary  is  properly  identified,  no  encroachment  or
violation of the Eco-Sensitive Zone can be presumed; and 
2

--- Page 220 ---
(iv) no violation has been found. The NGT has also imposed
costs of Rs. 20,000/- on the appellant.
4. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant, who has
placed reliance on subsequent proceedings of the Forest
Department,  which  were  not  the  subject  matter  of
consideration before the NGT.
5. We are not inclined to examine those proceedings for the
first  time  in  the  present  appeal.  It  is  open  to  the
appellant to approach the NGT by way of a review or other
appropriate application, as may be maintainable in law. We
express no opinion on the merits.
6. Insofar as the identification and demarcation of the
Nahargarh  reserved  forest  and  the  Nahargarh  Wildlife
Sanctuary  are  concerned,  the  matter  is  already  pending
before the High Court in the aforesaid writ petition, and
the appellant is at liberty to pursue his remedies therein.
7. It goes without saying that the High Court will consider
all the contentions that may be raised by the appellant, or
by any other public-spirited person, with respect to the
identification of the Nahargarh reserved forest and the
Nahargarh Wildlife Sanctuary. All concerned, including the
official respondents, shall abide by such determination,
subject to its attaining finality.
8. In the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case, the
costs of Rs. 20,000/- imposed on the appellant by the NGT
3

--- Page 221 ---
are set aside.
9. The  appeal  is,  accordingly,  disposed  of.  Pending
application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

                                VERSUS
ATUL KAKKAR                           Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Being aggrieved by the order dated 29.01.2026 in
TA-507-2025  and  TA-1365-2025,  passed  by  the  learned
Single Judge of the High Court of Punjab and Haryana at
Chandigarh, the appellant is before this Court.
3. The appellant is the wife of the respondent.
4. We have heard the appellant, who has appeared in
person  through  video  conferencing  facility  and  the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent. We have
also perused the material on record.
5. During the course of submission, learned counsel
appearing for the respondent submitted that the petition
filed by the respondent, namely, DMC/9/2025 titled “ Atul
Kakkar v. Neha Kakkar”  which was pending before the
Family  Court,  Ferozepur,  has  been  withdrawn  by  the
respondent.  Therefore,  TA-507-2025  filed  by  the
appellant herein has been rendered infructuous.
6. The appellant does not dispute this submission of
the learned counsel appearing for the respondent.

--- Page 234 ---
2
7. In such circumstances, we hold that TA-507-2025
has been rendered infructuous and no further orders are
called for on the said application.
8. As far as TA-1365-2025 filed by the appellant
herein seeking transfer of the petition filed under
Section 6 of the Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act,
1956  read  with  Sections  25,7,8,10  and  19  of  the
Guardians and Wards Act, 1890, i.e. GW/4/2025, titled
Neha Kakkar v. Atul Kakkar, seeking custody of the minor
daughter, which is pending on the file of the Family
Court, Ferozepur (Camp Court at Zira) is concerned, we
have heard the arguments made by the appellant and the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent.
9. Appellant submitted that she is working in HDFC
Life  in  Ludhiana  and  it  is  difficult  for  her  to
prosecute the petition filed by her in Zira, District
Ferozepur by travelling all the way from Ludhiana to
Zira. The appellant submitted that the said prayer may
be granted by this Court so that she could effectively
prosecute her petition seeking custody of the minor
daughter at Ludhiana itself.
10. However,  this  prayer  was  objected  to  by  the
learned counsel appearing for the respondent.  Learned
counsel appearing for the respondent contended that the
appellant is travelling to Zira for the purpose of
meeting the child and, therefore, she can very well

--- Page 235 ---
3
could prosecute her petition before the Family Court at
Zira.
11. In response  to this  submission, the  appellant
contended that it would be difficult for her to get
leave and travel from Ludhiana to Zira for the purpose
of prosecuting her petition.
12. We note that the said petition was filed at Zira
because the minor child resides at the said place along
with  the  respondent-husband.  However,  since  the
appellant resides at Ludhiana, she seeks transfer of the
said case from the Family Court, Ferozepur (Camp Court
at Zira) to the competent Court at District Ludhiana.  
13. We find force in the prayer sought for by the
appellant herein.
14. In  these  circumstances,  we  transfer  GW/4/2025
titled Neha Kakkar v. Atul Kakkar , pending before the
Principal Judge, Family Court, Ferozepur (Camp Court at
Zira)  to  the  Court  of  Competent  Jurisdiction  at
Ludhiana.
15. However, the respondent is at liberty to appear in
the said proceedings either in person or through video
conferencing facility.
16. If such a facility is sought for by the respondent
herein, the transferee Court shall make available the
said facility to the respondent.
17. The Registry of this Court to intimate this order
to both the Family Court, Ferozepur (Camp Court at Zira)

--- Page 236 ---
4
and the Court of Competent Jurisdiction (Family Court)
at Ludhiana.
18. The appeals stand disposed of in the aforesaid
terms.
19. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO  .  5298    /2026  
[@ SLP [CRL.] NO.  21976   /2026  ]
    [Diary No(s). 58699/2024]
AKSHAY & ORS.                        Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MAHARASHTRA & ANR.          Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. A limited issue has arisen in the present appeal
with regards to the withdrawal of amount deposited by
the deceased/accused. 
3. The present appellants are the legal heirs of
the deceased/accused, against whom Crime No.46/2023,
under Sections 255, 260, 420, 425, 465, 468, 471, 472
and 475 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; and Section
66D of the Information Technology (Amendment) Act,
2008 was registered. In the aforesaid case, at the
time of granting bail to the deceased/accused vide
order dated 20.09.2022, the High Court directed him
to deposit a sum of Rs.20,00,000/- which was duly
complied with by him. Thereafter, he passed away.
Thus, the proceedings qua the deceased got abated,
vide  order  of  the  concerned  Trial  Court  dated
04.01.2024.

--- Page 244 ---
2
4. Thereafter, the appellants filed an application
before the High Court to withdraw the aforestated sum
of Rs.20,00,000/- already deposited.
5. It was rejected by the High Court noting that
the interest of the complainant is vested in it.
Aggrieved, the present appellants are before us.
6. We  have  heard  the  submissions  made  by  the
learned counsel appearing for the parties.
7. In our considered view, the High Court has
committed  an  error  in  declining  the  request  to
withdraw the amount of Rs.20,00,000/-. Admittedly,
there is a difference between a criminal case and a
civil case. It is pertinent to note that a civil suit
filed by the complainant (Suit No.320/2023) is also
pending consideration.
8. It is a trite proposition of the criminal law
that the presumption of innocence is the foundational
principle of law involving a criminal offence. Also,
the earlier order was passed imposing the condition
only as a condition with respect to the grant of
bail.
9. Taking note of the above, we are inclined to set
aside the impugned order. 
10. Consequently, the appellants are permitted to
withdraw the amount deposited by the deceased.
11. Needless to state the order passed will have no

--- Page 245 ---
3
bearing on the pending civil suit.
12. The appeal stands allowed, accordingly.
13. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.
……………………………………………..J.
[M.M. SUNDRESH]
……………………………………………..J.
[PRASANNA B. VARALE]

stipulated time then the relief granted by this
Court shall be deemed to be withdrawn.”
5. When this matter came up before this Court for the first
time, the operation of the impugned order passed by the High
Court was stayed while issuing notice.
6. We take notice of the fact that at the relevant point of
time  when,  the  respondent-accused  preferred  the  petition
before the High Court, he was already declared as a proclaimed
absconder. The charge against him as indicative from the
allegations  reflected  in  the  FIR  appears  to  be  one  of
cheating, forgery, criminal conspiracy, etc.
7. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant would
submit  that  even  after the High Court granted indulgence to
2

--- Page 250 ---
the respondent-accused to surrender before the Trial Court
within two weeks, i.e., by 18.12.2025, till this date, he has
not surrendered.
8. We need not observe anything further.  
9. The impugned order is set aside.  The State is now
directed  to  proceed  further  to  apprehend  the  respondent-
accused and proceed with the measures to be taken after an
accused is being declared as a proclaimed absconder.  
10. With the aforesaid, the Appeal is disposed of.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
